title: Where Trees Give Up
question: What makes a climate polar, and how do its two types differ?
hook: One number, the average of the warmest month, decides whether a place can grow a forest at all.
idea: A polar climate has no month averaging 10 °C or more; if even one month tops 0 °C it is tundra, otherwise it is ice cap.

beats.prompt: A town's warmest month averages 12 °C, but its winters reach −40 °C. Is it a polar climate under Köppen?

choices.label: Yes, its winters are extremely cold
choices.feedback: Brutal winters alone do not decide it; polar climates are defined by the lack of a warm summer.

choices.label: Yes, because it must be near a pole
choices.feedback: Location is not the test; the monthly temperatures are.

beats.explain: A polar climate needs every month to average below 10 °C. With a 12 °C month, it falls outside the polar group despite cold winters.

beats.prompt: Sort each place into its polar climate type.
beats.explain: Ice cap places have no month above 0 °C and stay ice-covered; tundra places have at least one month above freezing.

beats.prompt: Match each polar climate feature to what it means.
beats.explain: Köppen labels polar climates E, splits them into ET and EF, and ties the 10 °C summer line to the tree line.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Ocean water in the Arctic can never drop below −2 °C.
That water, even under ice, keeps the Arctic warmer in winter.
This warm water is part of why Antarctica is much colder than the Arctic.
So the North Pole is the coldest place in the Northern Hemisphere.
beats.explain: The relatively warm ocean water keeps the North Pole from being the coldest place in the Northern Hemisphere, and helps explain why Antarctica is much colder.
